A supporter of President Donald Trump punched a heckler wearing a "Release the Epstein Files" shirt at the president's Youngstown, Ohio, rally.

A heckler wearing a "Release the Epstein Files" shirt was punched in the face by an apparent supporter of President Donald Trump during a rally Monday in Youngstown, Ohio, before the president mocked the protester's weight.

Trump was criticizing Ohio Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted after losing his Senate seat in 2024, when rally attendees shifted their attention toward a confrontation in the crowd.

Video of the confrontation showed a rallygoer who appeared to support Trump shoving the heckler and striking her in the face as the crowd chanted "USA!"

Trump Touts ‘Golden Age’ At Ohio Rally, Urges Voters To Deliver Gop Midterm Wins

The man also grabbed the woman by the hair and attempted to slam her face toward the ground.

Police eventually intervened and broke up the fight before escorting the woman out of the venue. Video showed the man who struck her remaining in the arena and exchanging high-fives with other attendees.

Read On The Fox News App

Advertisement

Trump appeared to notice the disruption and accused the protester of being paid to interrupt the rally, although he offered no evidence to support the allegation. He also mocked the protester's weight.

Anti-trump Protester Charged After Viral Video Appears To Show Journalist Shoved At Maine Protest

"He's a paid protester," Trump said, appearing to be unaware that the heckler was a woman. "They’re all paid. They get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They’re scum. But he’s going back home to Mom. He’s going back home to Mom. Look at him. Look at him. Terrible. Don’t we love law enforcement? Oh, he’s gotta go on a diet! He’s a fat guy. Wow. Wow. Gotta go on a diet fast. We all do."

"No, they’re paid protesters. That’s a very low-class protester," the president added.

The woman's "Release the Epstein Files" shirt comes as Trump and his Justice Department face bipartisan scrutiny over the delay in the release of additional documents related to the investigations into deceased sex predator Jeffrey Epstein.

Just days before the fight on Monday, there was a fight at another Trump rally in San Antonio, Texas, where a man wearing a MAGA hat grabbed a heckler by the hair and pulled him to the ground.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Donald Trump Rejects Claims Russia and China Are Aiding Iran and Insists Superpowers Have 'Too Much To Lose'

Trump dismisses claims of Russia and China helping Iran, prompting questions about his earlier warnings, US sanctions and online reaction.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump rejected allegations of Russia and China helping Iran on Monday, 12 October, saying both countries had 'too much to lose.'

His 'Truth Social' statement drew online criticism and renewed questions about what Washington knows about Tehran's foreign support, as it contained no explicit threat of retaliation.

The remarks followed months of war between Iran and the United States and Israel, which began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February. They also followed Trump's July warning that Russian or Chinese involvement would be 'very bad for them.' The October post was less direct about any consequences.

Trump began by calling those raising the allegations 'Radical Left Morons and Lunatics.' He sarcastically referred to the 'wonderful' Islamic Republic of Iran, with the adjective enclosed in quotation marks.

'If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all,' he wrote on Truth Social. 'They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!'

Trump offered no evidence to support his assessment or explain what Russia and China stood to lose. He also didn't say whether the US had detected weapons transfers, intelligence-sharing, or another form of assistance. His words expressed confidence without identifying its basis.

In a 24 July 'Truth Social' statement, he said he had received assurances from Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to Trump, Xi promised that neither China nor Chinese companies would supply weapons to Iran. He said Putin had offered a similar assurance.

'If they did, it would be very bad for them,' Trump warned at the time. The reported assurances were his account of the leaders' conversations, not independently verified commitments.

That earlier warning also followed questions inside Washington. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told US senators in July that Russia and China were enabling some Iranian activities at different levels, without specifying how.

Reuters reported that US intelligence was examining possible Russian assistance with targeting information or drone technology.

The October statement did not address those concerns directly. It also left open whether Trump meant only direct government involvement or assistance through private companies.

Washington has already alleged that foreign procurement networks helped Iran obtain weapons and materials. On 8 May, the US Treasury Department sanctioned 10 individuals and companies across several countries. It said the targets had supported Iranian efforts to secure weapons and materials for drones and ballistic missiles.

The department announced further sanctions on 10 June against nine individuals and entities. The targets included China- and Hong Kong-based firms and people allegedly involved in weapons procurement and related transactions for Iranian military organisations.

Those sanctions describe accusations against specific businesses and individuals. They do not, by themselves, prove that the Chinese or Russian governments are directing military assistance to Iran.

A US congressional commission has separately documented China's economic, technological and diplomatic relationship with Tehran. Its account shows that support can extend beyond direct arms sales. Beijing has opposed US sanctions and called for negotiations over the war.

Trump: “I see so many comments from the Radical Left Morons and Lunatics that China and Russia are helping the ‘wonderful’ Islamic Republic of Iran. If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it,… pic.twitter.com/z30FdyBkzz

Discussion of Trump's latest statement spread online. In a Reddit thread linking to coverage of his remarks, one commenter challenged the description of an 'unhinged threat,' asking where such a threat appeared. Another replied, 'It's low-level, but still a threat.'

The exchange captured competing interpretations rather than public opinion. The selected comments cannot establish how Americans broadly view Trump's words, much less how Moscow or Beijing understood them.

Trump's post announced no new sanctions, deadline or military action. His July warning was sharper, while existing US sanctions concern alleged activities that his latest message did not address. Whether either government is currently helping Iran remains a separate question from what the president believes.

And his critics were totally there for it.

The president said:

“You know, if they get in and you have a bad presidential election in the next, because we have some very good people. But if you had a bad presidential where one of these lunatics got in, you will, look at me right now, and you will say, ‘He’s going to be the last Republican president in the history of our country.’ I will be. I will be. I will be the last Republican president because they will add about 12 more electoral votes. They’ll add four more senators. They’ll add 10 more congresspeople, approximately. They’re gonna rig the Supreme Court through just a lot of people. They want to put a lot of people.”
